narrative:
The model predicted an 82% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess likely success in law school and beyond, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. At 24, it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling weaker preparation in the skills the bar exam tests. Next, your third-year class ranking played a major role, also pulling the outcome toward failure. Placing in the second decile compared to an average of nearly sixth among accepted students showed that your academic performance in law school lagged behind most successful applicants. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked mildly in the opposite direction, offering a small positive signal because it was not as low as other elements of your profile.

Taken together, these academic indicators outweighed other details such as your middle-income background, full-time status, gender, and race, none of which factored into the model.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT and aiming for a substantially higher score, combined with targeted bar-prep courses that address the specific gaps reflected in your class rank, would be the clearest next steps before reapplying.
